# 1 Chronicles Chapter 20 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 380v–381r

---

**1** In the spring, the season when kings march out to war, Joab led the army out and devastated Ammonite territory. He advanced to Rabbah and besieged it — while David stayed behind in Jerusalem. Joab captured Rabbah and demolished it.

**2** David took the crown from the head of the Ammonite king. It weighed a talent of gold and was set with a precious stone. It was placed on David's own head. He also hauled off an enormous amount of plunder from the city.

**3** As for the people in the city, he brought them out and put them to work with saws, iron tools, and axes. David did this to every Ammonite town. Then David and the entire army returned to Jerusalem.

**4** Later, fighting broke out with the Philistines at Gezer. During that battle Sibbecai the Hushathite killed Sippai, a descendant of the ancient giants, and the Philistines were crushed.

**5** In another battle with the Philistines, Elhanan son of Jair killed Lahmi, the brother of Goliath of Gath, whose spear had a shaft as thick as a weaver's beam.

**6** Yet another battle took place at Gath. A huge man fought there who had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot — twenty-four altogether. He too was descended from the giants.

**7** When he mocked Israel, Jonathan — the son of Shimea, David's brother — struck him down.

**8** These giants of Gath all fell at the hands of David and his men.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 1 — The silence that shouts:** "David stayed behind in Jerusalem." In 2 Samuel, these words open the most devastating chapter of David's life — the affair with Bathsheba, the betrayal and murder of Uriah, Nathan's searing rebuke, the death of the child. The Chronicler erases all of it. Not a word. Not a hint. The reader of Chronicles alone would never know that David's greatest sin occurred precisely here, in this gap between Joab's departure and Rabbah's fall. This is not merely selective history — it is theological editing of the highest order. The Chronicler needs a David worthy of the temple, and so the David of 2 Samuel 11-12 ceases to exist. The question this raises is profound: Can a story be truthful when it omits the truth?

**Verse 2 — The crown:** A talent of gold weighs roughly 75 pounds — far too heavy to wear. This may be ceremonial placement, or the weight may be symbolic rather than literal. Either way, the image is vivid: the crown of a conquered king on David's head.

**Verse 5 — Goliath's brother:** The Chronicler solves one of the Bible's famous contradictions. David killed Goliath (1 Samuel 17). But 2 Samuel 21:19 says Elhanan killed Goliath. The Chronicler's solution: Elhanan killed Goliath's *brother*, named Lahmi. Whether this is historical memory or editorial harmonization, it reveals a biblical author actively managing his tradition.

*— PNEUMA*
